etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Latin trītus (“worn out”), perfect passive participle of terō (“to wear away, wear out”).
senses: (often in reference to a word or phrase) used so many times that it is commonplace, or no longer interesting or effective; worn out, hackneyed.
(law) So well established as to be beyond debate: trite law.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
senses: A denomination of coinage in ancient Greece equivalent to one third of a stater.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
paragraphs: Unadapted borrowing from Latin tritē, from Ancient Greek τρίτη (trítē, literally “third [string]”).
senses: (music, music theory) In Ancient Greek musical theory, the lower-pitched of the two movable notes in the farther tetrachord on a lyre, pitched lower than the paranete and higher than the paramese.
